articles.title: France deploys 70,000 police officers to prepare for new wave of protests on Halloween
articles.summary: Emmanuel Macron's government deploys 70,000 police officers as France braces for a third week of intense protests amid over $1 billion in losses.
articles.body: The French government is deploying 70,000 police officers to cities across the country as authorities expect a third week of intense anti-government protests to resume Saturday. Demonstrators objecting to rising costs and President Emmanuel Macron's government have engaged in looting and damaging property, prompting the law enforcement surge, according to officials. "Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble," Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said at a news conference early in the week. FRANCE ON EDGE WITH 70,000 POLICE DEPLOYED FOR UNREST AS AUTHORITIES PROBE SUSPECTED TERROR ATTACK NEAR PARIS The expected protests, coinciding with Halloween, introduce an additional element to authorities' response, as some protesters are expected to don Halloween masks to hide their identities. At least 150 planned gatherings across the country have been tracked and acknowledged by the Interior Ministry.Videos circulating on social media Saturday appeared to show fresh confrontations as anti-government protests continued across France, despite the deployment of 70,000 police officers nationwide. In Paris, video posted to X by journalist Oliya Scootercaster appeared to show an object being thrown toward a group of riot police as officers moved through a street. Scootercaster identified the object as a Molotov cocktail. Meanwhile, a separate video shared on X by the account Bleu Blanc Rouge purported to show protesters breaking into a residential building in Marseille. The video showed a crowd gathered near a building entrance. FRANCE'S MACRON BLAMES PROTESTS ON 'ULTRA-LEFT GROUPS WHOSE AIM IS TO BRING DOWN THE REPUBLIC' One of the events, a planned march between the iconic Parisian squares of Republique and Bastille, has been banned by France's top administrative court. The demonstration was instead rerouted to boulevards on the eastern fringe of the city, far from the main shopping centers. France's Chamber of Commerce has estimated retail losses from looting and property damage at over $1 billion, while other estimates that include lost revenue calculate losses could be double that. PHOTOS SHOW AFTERMATH OF RIOTS AS MASKED GROUPS CLASH WITH POLICE ACROSS FRANCE Some of Paris' iconic luxury shops, like Hermes and Louis Vuitton, have been targeted by rioters as France's marquee shopping avenues now show scores of buildings with protective wooden boards. In response to the unrest, France's government is crafting a law that would punish rioters who caused property damage and make them liable to pay up to €10,000, or $11,000. VIOLENCE ERUPTS AT FRANCE PROTESTS AS MACRON WARNS UNREST IS BEING EXPLOITED Demonstrations originated with the country's young people protesting schooling conditions and pushing for educational reform and quickly ballooned to include other social groups and issues, including economic anxieties, rising costs in fuel and borrowing. Though the French government has vowed to reform education and reduce fuel costs, the promises have not satisfied the protesters. "When I was little, I was told young people were the future," 15-year-old high school student Aaron Berthier de Grandry, who plans on protesting over the weekend, told Reuters. "Well, if we, as the future of France, lack resources, that means France will end up collapsing," de Grandry added. The U.S. Embassy in France has advised travelers to avoid areas where large gatherings are taking place. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed puts ministers through military training
articles.summary: The prime minister has previously emphasised military preparedness as central to his government's ambitions.
articles.body:
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put his cabinet ministers and other senior government officials through military training, saying armed forces discipline can help build stronger leaders and advance the country's development.

Photos shared by him on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre.

The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials are rarely seen undergoing military training.

Those taking part include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba.

It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last.

In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia's ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable.

He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership.

"Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory," he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both.

Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives.

The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia.

It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries.

Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions.

articles.title: Haunted, but hardly explored: India's untapped ghost-tourism economy
articles.summary: India's ghosts have a customer service problem.
articles.body: India's ghosts have a customer service problem.There is almost an abundance of local places which have a reputation of being haunted in each and every state.There are ghost villages where nobody is quite sure why everyone left. Forts with stories of spirits walking through them at night. Abandoned cemeteries as old as the world wars, forgotten ‘havelis’ and stretches of forest that have acquired a mythology of their own.Out of all these only a few have become tourist attractions; others survive largely through word of mouth, local lore and the occasional paranormal investigation.India's haunted places do have an audience but it somehow lacks a concrete machinery that could make ‘dark’ tourism and ‘spectral’ cities central factions of an ever growing tourist economy.The business of the macabreThe tourism industry has a name for this particular appetite for the unsettling: dark tourism. The term broadly describes travel to places associated with death, tragedy, violence and suffering.Ghost tours, haunted heritage walks and visits to places associated with paranormal folklore occupy a more specialised corner of this spectrum, where history, local legend and the promise of an eerie experience often intersect.It is an appetite that the tourism industry has increasingly tried to package. Turning a city's darker history into something you can book online. And its most ideal form, the ticket buys you a completely immersive tour full of storytelling with a slight hope of encountering your first paranormal spirit.The commercial potential of dark tourism is reflected in the market estimates. Grand View Research valued the global dark tourism market at $31.8 billion in 2023 and projects it to reach $34.2 billion in 2026 and $38.6 billion by 2030, growing at a compound annual growth rate of 2.9%. MR puts the market at $32 billion in 2025, forecasting it to reach $46.8 billion by 2036.The market for ghost tourism as a separate entity is estimated to be worth $2.9 billion in 2025 and projects it to grow to $5.7 billion by 2034, at a CAGR of 7.8%, by Dataintelo. Its estimate includes guided ghost walks, cemetery and underground tours, paranormal investigations, haunted stays and virtual experiences.For India, the more immediate question may be less about capturing a share of a global market and more about whether these scattered attractions can be turned into viable profitable local experiences. With a history as rich as ours, the ghosts are not in short supply. The challenge is to turn them into profitable experiences that people can discover, book and pay for, while ensuring that the tragedy is respected and the communities living alongside these places have a stake in the business.From a haunted reputation to a tourism productKuldhara, a site that Rajasthan Tourism itself promotes as a “ghost village shrouded in mystery”, is a good starting point. The official government site describes its history as a prosperous settlement abandoned in the early 19th century. The account recounts the popular legend involving the village headman's daughter and the powerful minister Salim Singh, while also identifying the ruins as a protected monument under the state archaeology department.The village, around 17km from Jaisalmer, already has the ingredients of a tourism attraction, but having a story and having a well-managed visitor experience are two different things.There are multiple accounts of litter around the site, including discarded plastic and food packaging. How can an atmosphere feel haunted when the landscape is strewn with chips and tobacco packets?And cleanliness isn’t the only issue. Talking to two people who visited the site, the common experience has been mismanaged and under researched tour which leaves most customers underwhelmed at the end of the day.Bhangarh, in Alwar district, is often described as one of India's most haunted places. Rajasthan Tourism itself recounts the two popular legends attached to the site: one involving the ascetic Baba Balu Nath, whose warning about the shadow of the fort was allegedly ignored, and another about a sorcerer whose failed attempt to enchant Princess Ratnavati supposedly led him to curse the town.The legends have become part of the destination's appeal, drawing visitors to its ruined temples, palaces and deserted marketplace. The restriction on entry before sunrise and after sunset, imposed at the site, has only added to its mystique. But tourists who visit the site have also called it unorganised, speaking to TOI they noted that the guide also was not entirely accurate about the historical aspects of the site and the site itself needed to have better management.The business of making a place come aliveThere are already attempts to package India's haunted heritage into guided experiences. Delhi Tourism lists Haunted Heritage Walks at Malcha Mahal and Feroz Shah Kotla Monument, each lasting around 90 minutes and available on weekends on group demand. The official booking page lists a minimum group size of six and a tariff of Rs 800 plus GST per person.The Ministry of Tourism's Utsav portal has also listed a Haunted Walk at Bhuli Bhatiyari, organised by Delhi-based Enroute Indian History. The listing describes a guided heritage walk through the old hunting lodge, combining its history with the legends associated with the site.Enroute Indian History, which has been conducting the experience for around two to three years, says the walks attract a good number of bookings and are designed for adventure seekers as much as for history enthusiasts. The operator says it takes care to keep the historical information accurate, while folklore and supernatural accounts are presented as stories rather than fact-checked historical claims. This distinction is central to the format: visitors are offered a combination of documented history, local legends and the possibility of an unsettling experience.These initiatives complicate the idea that haunted tourism in India is entirely informal or absent. There are government-backed products and private operators working in the space. The question is whether they have developed the consistency, visibility and scale needed to make haunted experiences a dependable part of a destination's tourism economy.Ghost is only part of the experienceDetailing her experience to TOI, Kriti notes that she remembers the underground setting of the haunted heritage walk she took in Edinburgh as much as the stories themselves. The interactive displays and historical details provided by the guide gave the experience a sense of depth that a conventional ghost walk might not have offered.A ghost tour can take several forms, the attraction lies as much in how visitors encounter the story as in the story itself.A 2020 study published in Cornell Hospitality Quarterly, titled Paranormal Tourism: Market Study of a Novel and Interactive Approach to Space Activation and Monetization, makes this case through examples from the United States and elsewhere. It describes how destinations such as New Orleans combine ghost stories with local histories and cultural associations, while Salem packages its reputation around witches and ghosts. These places do not necessarily sell a standalone encounter with the paranormal; they draw on identities and histories that visitors may already associate with them.The study talks in detail about Eastern State Penitentiary in Philadelphia, a former prison that closed in 1971 and subsequently fell into disuse. Limited group tours began in 1988 as part of efforts to preserve the site. A Halloween fundraiser followed in 1991, eventually developing into the annual attraction Terror Behind the Walls. By 1994, the former prison was also offering daily historical tours to generate income for preservation, followed by museum exhibits and a broader marketing campaign.The study also points to the role of participation in making these experiences engaging. The experience can continue beyond the visit itself, with reviews, photographs and word of mouth helping to draw in new audiences.Research into British ghost walks suggests that the appeal is not necessarily dependent on visitors believing in ghosts. An ethnographic study of 14 tours across Edinburgh, York, London and Brighton found that guides use a combination of storytelling, performance and the physical environment to make history tangible.For India, that distinction could be important. A haunted experience need not rely on sensational claims. It can be built around the history of a place, the folklore that has accumulated around it and the atmosphere of encountering that story on location.Local community cannot remain part of the backdropThe opportunity, however, is not simply to make India's haunted sites more theatrical or commercially attractive. It is also to ensure that the people and places behind the stories are not left out of the value chain.A 2023 qualitative study of local perceptions in Kuldhara, based on 25 interviews with residents and people working in the area, found that respondents saw several economic opportunities in developing mystery and paranormal tourism. Some respondents also pointed to existing livelihood opportunities linked to visitors, including guiding, transport and the sale of local crafts.The study also recorded expectations around the restoration and preservation of the village, alongside concerns about the role of government and private bodies in developing the destination. While it offers a glimpse of how residents view the possibilities of mystery tourism, it does not quantify how much income currently reaches the community or how widely those benefits are distributed.The concerns are not unique to haunted destinations. A 2026 study of tourism in Uttarakhand, while not focused specifically on ghost tourism, raises wider questions about the state's tourism economy. It argues for stronger community participation, local supply chains, training and livelihood diversification.These concerns are relevant when considering how niche tourism experiences might develop in the hills. A haunted walk could create work for local storytellers, drivers, homestays, food vendors and artisans. But those benefits are not automatic. If an outside operator controls the bookings, supplies the guides and takes most of the revenue, the local community may remain little more than a feature of the landscape.The challenge is to move beyond treating local legends as raw material that can be packaged elsewhere. Residents may be the custodians of oral histories, but they should also have a stake in how those histories are interpreted and monetised.India does not need to manufacture a haunted history. What it needs is a way to bring those stories to visitors without reducing them to cheap thrills or leaving the people who have preserved them out of the business.The real test of India's haunted tourism economy will not be how many people it can convince that a place is haunted, but how many people it can persuade to stay, listen, and explore.The ghosts, after all, have been doing their bit for the tourism industry for years. It is time someone took care of the guests.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Pope Leo tells Villanova and Notre Dame basketball teams he is neutral. Prevost has other ideas
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV on Saturday told the basketball teams from his alma mater Villanova and fellow Catholic university Notre Dame — in Rome for their season opener — that in matters of sport, the pontiff is neutral.
articles.body: VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV on Saturday told the basketball teams from his alma mater Villanova and fellow Catholic university Notre Dame — in Rome for their season opener — that in matters of sport, the pontiff is neutral. Then the pope, who was born Robert Prevost, said his former self might disagree. “Prevost has another opinion, but we won’t do that now,” he said to laughs during a whooping, cheering audience of 7,000 people from both schools — players, coaches, fans and their families — in the Vatican audience hall. The teams were in town for the U.S. college basketball season opener in Rome. The Villanova and Notre Dame men’s and women’s teams will play a doubleheader on Sunday at the 11,000-seat Palazzo dello Sport, about a half-hour drive from the Vatican. The event has been dubbed the Eternal City Tip-Off and was created to honor the first American pope. The audience had been up in the air after the 71-year-old pope underwent lung cancer surgery on Oct. 13 and is still recovering. But Leo kept the appointment ahead of Sunday’s opener. Leo graduated in 1977 with a Bachelor of Science in mathematics from Villanova, the Augustinian school near Philadelphia. He was born in Chicago — not all that far from Notre Dame, which is located in South Bend, Indiana. Leo dribbles and poses Leo, an avid sports fan and tennis player, dribbled a golden basketball presented to him by the Villanova women’s team. And when the towering players from Notre Dame presented him with a jersey and another golden ball, Leo stepped up to the podium where his chair sits to try to gain a few inches (centimeters) on them. He gamely posed for a photo with the Fighting Irish, holding the banner they gave him “Pope Leo, Play like a champion today” — a riff on the famous Notre Dame sign at the university stairwell between the locker room and the stadium. But he gave Villanova equal time, making the “V’” gesture with his hand as chants of “Let’s Go ‘Nova” erupted in the audience hall. Sport as a way to saintliness After mistakenly starting out in Italian, Leo switched to his mother-tongue English and spoke off the cuff, recalling that in his native Chicago, he grew up hearing “Go Irish,” the Notre Dame chant. “But as you all know, Prevost graduated from Villanova,” Leo said, referring to his past self in the third person. “So the pope doesn’t take sides,” he said to laughs, before revealing that “Prevost has another opinion.” In his prepared remarks to the crowd, Leo urged the teams and their families to embrace sports as a way to grow in saintliness. “No one is born a champion, just as no one is born a saint,” Leo said. He warned against letting sporting rivalries get out of hand and he said he hoped the fans in Rome this weekend would actually get to know one another as they cheer, “even passionately.” “In any competition, the members of two teams, even when they have a competitive rivalry, are certainly not enemies,” he said. “I hope, therefore, that despite the competitive nature of college basketball, there will be opportunities for the players and the fans of both teams to get to know each other in your days here in Rome.” He noted that the game will take place on All Saints’ Day, and that the church teaches Christians to pursue saintliness in every aspect of their lives, including in sports. “Our true goal, beyond emerging victorious in any one event, is to win the prize of everlasting life,” he said. Leo and past popes have exalted sports Like popes before him, Leo has praised the value of sport for both physical and spiritual development, calling sport a “school of fraternity” that nurtures friendship, respect and teamwork. But he also warned about how the win-at-all-cost mentality of sport has contributed to episodes of doping, match-fixing and other forms of corruption. The Rev. Robert Dowd, president of Notre Dame, acknowledged Villanova had something of an edge in Sunday’s game, considering it counts the pope as an alumnus. But in an interview Saturday, he said the occasion to bring both teams together with all their fans in Rome for a papal audience and season opener was “amazing.” “I know that the pope is a pope for all of us, and so I’m grateful,” he said. “I know in a particular way the pope talks about the importance of bridge building, and I’m sure he’ll be a bridge builder when we play each other.” Villanova’s president, the Rev. Peter M. Donohue, said there was “a little extra pride” being with Leo, given his allegiance. But he said what happens on Sunday was not the point. “No matter what happens on the court, this is the true highlight of the trip,” he said in his introductory remarks to the audience. “Tomorrow we will cheer, we will compete, but today we are simply grateful.” Philadelphia Archbishop Nelson Perez celebrated a private Mass for traveling fans in St. Peter’s Basilica on Saturday morning, and asked the thousands of people in the pews to give a round of applause to the players. The English-language liturgy was unusual in that it had all the trappings of a papal Mass celebrated at the main altar and televised live by Vatican Media. Leo is an avid Chicago White Sox fan, and has been known to follow basketball, too. Asked about the upcoming games on the papal plane during a recent trip to France, Leo said, “They tell me that the people coming to the match, 90% are Villanova and 10% Notre Dame, so the voice of the people of God will be very strong on the Villanova side.”

articles.title: A Georgia software developer says he was promised 30% of profits from a joint venture in 2018; after the relationship broke down, an October 29 appeals ruling found no enforceable partnership and rejected his claims
articles.summary: A business arrangement built around the promise of a share in future software profits ended in a legal dispute after a Georgia technology company
articles.body: A business arrangement built around the promise of a share in future software profits ended in a legal dispute after a Georgia technology company terminated its relationship with a software developer. The developer claimed he had been promised 30% of the profits from products created by a joint venture, along with an opportunity to operate the venture using his intellectual property. However, the business owner maintained that the proposed partnership was never formally established and that the developer had already been paid a salary for his work.The Georgia Court of Appeals has now sided with the company and its owner, reversing a lower court's decision that had allowed several of the developer's claims to proceed. The October 29, 2026, ruling in Bruce Mortimer et al. v. Jeff White, available on Justia, found that the parties never reached an enforceable agreement to form a partnership because essential terms remained unresolved. The court also rejected the developer's alternative claims involving unpaid services, intellectual property and alleged trade secrets violations.A 2018 promise to share software profitsThe dispute began in 2018, when Jeff White joined RutterKey Solutions LLC (RKS), a technology services company owned by Bruce Mortimer. White worked as the company's Chief Technology Officer and Vice-President of Product Development, with the responsibility of building an in-house team to develop and license software solutions. According to White, he and Mortimer discussed creating a separate joint venture through which they would develop and commercialise software products. In December 2018, they allegedly reached an oral agreement to establish a limited liability company, with White receiving 30% of the venture's profits and permission to operate it using his intellectual property.White later relied on a 2022 letter of intent (LOI), which referred to a mutual understanding to establish a partnership for product development under the RKS brand. It also described a proposed 70-30 division of profits from software licensing or intellectual property sales, with White receiving the smaller share. However, the document stated that the partnership's final form and structure would be decided later with professional guidance.Relationship breaks down after five yearsThe working relationship continued until September 2023, when Mortimer terminated White's association with the company, reportedly citing insubordination. White subsequently filed a lawsuit in October 2023, alleging breach of contract, conversion of intellectual property, trade secrets violations, promissory estoppel and other claims. He argued that Mortimer and RKS had failed to establish the promised company, share profits or allow him to operate the proposed venture.Mortimer and RKS disputed the allegations, arguing that no separate partnership had ever been created. Mortimer said he had considered a joint venture as a way to incentivise White's work but eventually decided to manage the product development activities entirely through RKS. He also maintained that White would receive an incentive equivalent to 30% of net profits from qualifying products developed by White and his team. However, according to Mortimer, the products generated no net profits that would make White eligible for the payment.Court finds essential partnership terms were missingThe central question before the appeals court was whether the discussions and subsequent letter of intent amounted to an enforceable contract. The judges found that they did not. For a contract to be legally enforceable under Georgia law, the parties must agree on its essential terms with sufficient certainty. An agreement to negotiate or finalise important details later is not enough. The court pointed to several unresolved issues, including how the venture would operate, how expenses and revenues would be allocated, when profits would be distributed and which software products would qualify for profit-sharing.White also acknowledged that the parties had never settled whether he would have decision-making or veto rights as a 30% owner. His own emails showed that the arrangement's terms and the proposed LLC had remained unsettled. The court therefore concluded that the evidence established only an agreement to agree, not an enforceable partnership or joint venture.Salary and intellectual property claims also rejectedThe appeals court also dismissed White's alternative claim for compensation under quantum meruit, a legal principle allowing recovery for valuable services when withholding payment would be unjust. The record showed that RKS had employed White from 2019 through 2023, paying him an annual salary ranging from approximately $171,000 to $252,000. The court found no evidence establishing that this salary failed to compensate him reasonably for his work.His intellectual property and trade secrets claims also failed. The judges noted that White had been treated as an employee, received a salary, had taxes withheld and reported his income through a W-2 form. Under the work-for-hire doctrine, intellectual property created by an employee within the scope of employment generally belongs to the employer for copyright purposes. The court further found that White had not specifically identified the intellectual property he wanted returned, despite the company's attorney offering to return any property he could properly identify.On October 29, 2026, the Georgia Court of Appeals reversed the lower court's denial of summary judgment on White's remaining claims, including breach of contract, promissory estoppel, quantum meruit, conversion and trade secrets violations. The ruling also disposed of his related requests for punitive damages, attorney fees and injunctive relief. The ruling illustrates that discussions about future profit-sharing, even when recorded in a letter of intent, may not create an enforceable partnership when fundamental business terms remain undecided.You use AI every day. articles.title: Can a woman be friends with a hot guy without being romantic? Expert pinpoints warning signs
articles.summary: The Nora Ephron debate from "When Harry Met Sally" resurfaces as an expert reveals when platonic friendships quietly become emotional affairs.
articles.body: The question of whether men and women can remain "just friends" drew fresh attention when Jenny McCarthy and her husband, Donnie Wahlberg, recently bantered on her podcast about whether having an attractive male friend crosses a line. Attraction alone doesn’t necessarily threaten a friendship, according to Susan Trombetti, relationship expert and CEO of Exclusive Matchmaking in Maryland. However, unspoken feelings and growing emotional intimacy can blur boundaries, she told Fox News Digital. 5 MARRIAGE MISTAKES COUPLES MAKE WITHOUT REALIZING IT — AND HOW TO AVOID THEM "I think we can be friends with hot people … but a lot of times, I believe that friendship started with a sexual interest or romantic interest, and the timing wasn't right or the other person wasn't interested in them." Some people may maintain friendships while leaving open the possibility of a future romantic relationship, Trombetti said. "I don't think women and men can ever truly be friends," she told Fox News Digital. "I think it was always a sexual undertone that sparked the friendship and a foot-in-the-door for something more, [even if] it's 20 years from now." YOUNGER MEN ARE ATTRACTED TO OLDER WOMEN FOR REASONS THAT HAVE NOTHING TO DO WITH LOOKS Trombetti said recognizing that someone is handsome doesn’t necessarily lead to feeling chemistry with that person — and finding a friend attractive does not, on its own, constitute infidelity. The problem, she said, is when harmless awareness turns into an emotional affair. "The line between attraction with a friend and an emotional affair is a slippery slope, especially if you have a partner," the expert cautioned. articles.title: Cardiff solicitor defrauds Cancer Research UK of thousands
articles.summary: The money paid to Michael Fogg could have been used by Cancer Research UK to pay for 48 biopsies.
articles.body:
A solicitor defrauded a cancer charity out of thousands of pounds after submitting fake invoices for work he had not carried out, a court heard.

Michael Fogg, 47, of Cyncoed, Cardiff, offered his services to Cancer Research UK's free will writing scheme, but when the charity contacted people he claimed to represent, they said they had not used the solicitor.

The hearing was told the money it lost as a result of Fogg's actions could have paid for 48 biopsies.

He was sentenced to 10 months' imprisonment, suspended for two years in a hearing at Newport Crown Court on Friday.

An investigation was launched by Cancer Research UK after emails and addresses for Fogg's clients were found to be non-existent.

Judge Carl Harrison said: "You had a position in the legal profession which allowed you to fund your greed."

The court heard that Cancer Research UK has been operating its scheme for 25 years, providing people with access to a free will writing service.

Solicitors employed through the scheme can charge the charity £120 plus VAT for an individual will and £170 plus VAT for mirror wills, which are wills which mirror each other which can be taken out by couples.

Prosecutor Charles Archer said Fogg and his company Trusting Willpower Ltd joined the free will service in 2021.

On 6 July 2023, Cancer Research UK legal partnership manager Kelly Brooks raised concerns to counter-fraud manager Phil Sapey about the defendant's services.

The charity provides thank you cards to members who pledge more than £100 to Cancer Research UK in their will, but alarm bells rang when 32 cards were sent out to individuals that Fogg said he had drafted wills for.

Some of the people who received cards responded to say they had not had wills drafted by Fogg.

The defendant was asked for an explanation and he said he had received instructions to prepare wills on behalf of the individuals referred to.

Trusting Willpower Ltd invoiced Cancer Research UK for £29,090. The charity had paid £18,150 to the company but withheld the rest of the payments until clarification had been received.

Cancer Research UK sent 250 emails to individuals which Trusting Willpower Ltd claimed they had written wills for, but 58 of the emails were undeliverable, suggesting they were invalid.

Nine people responded saying they had not used Fogg's services, and were not living at the address provided.

After further investigations, the charity attempted to contact more clients in respect of 260 wills.

Eight people responded saying they had used the defendant's services to write a will, but 41 said they had not used his services.

The court heard 172 clients were found to have invalid phone numbers and 38 people had invalid email addresses.

The matter was reported to the police and Fogg was arrested. In his police interview he denied defrauding the charity and answered "no comment" to questions.

Archer said the total fraud was based on 40 invoices and amounted to £4,800.

The prosecutor said the defendant's behaviour amounted to an "abuse of trust and responsibility" as a solicitor.

The court heard that Fogg was of previous good character.

In a victim personal statement, Sapey said Cancer Research UK received no benefit from the free will service and the false claims made by Fogg represented funds that would have been used towards curing cancer and providing support to people diagnosed with the disease.

In mitigation, James Tucker said the Cancer Research UK's work should be "applauded" and his client felt "deeply ashamed" of his behaviour.

The barrister said the defendant was a family man and a parent, with a number of health issues including a brain injury, epilepsy, anxiety and depression.

The defendant no longer works as a solicitor.

Fogg, who pleaded guilty to fraud by false representation at an earlier hearing, was also ordered to carry out a 24-day rehabilitation activity requirement and 120 hours unpaid work.

articles.body: Dozens of Afghan migrants detained in the United States are expected to be deported as early as next week, potentially including relatives of Afghans who worked alongside American military forces during the war in Afghanistan. The planned removals have sparked alarm among immigration lawyers, refugee advocacy groups and families, who fear those sent back could face persecution or torture under Taliban rule.According to lawyers, advocacy groups and relatives of detained migrants, dozens of Afghans are expected to be deported early next week. A court filing reviewed by ABC News in the case of one Afghan immigrant indicates that a deportation flight scheduled for next week is expected to take the individual to Pakistan, followed by further transportation to Afghanistan.Advocates and families have previously told ABC News that hundreds of Afghan immigrants are currently being held in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facilities in Louisiana. Many international deportation flights depart from the state.Families fear relatives could face Taliban persecutionThe possible deportations have heightened anxiety among families, particularly those whose relatives have connections to the US military or government.Charlotte Moyal told ABC News that her husband, who has been in immigration detention for more than a year, was recently transferred from a detention facility in Pennsylvania to one in Louisiana.Moyal said her husband was informed that he could be deported from the United States as early as next week.Families fear that if their relatives are ultimately sent to Afghanistan, they could face torture or persecution from the Taliban because of their association with the United States.Shawn VanDiver, founder and president of AfghanEvac, a nonprofit organisation supporting Afghans evacuated from their home country following the US withdrawal, said families of those detained were terrified."Anybody from Afghanistan is in danger if they get sent back," VanDiver told ABC News.US administration defends immigration policyThe US State Department defended the administration's position on immigration and deportations.A department spokesperson said earlier this week that the US maintained its position that "all countries must be able to manage their borders and immigration processes in a manner that ensures the safety, security, and prosperity of their citizens."However, the possibility of deporting Afghans who assisted American forces has drawn criticism from Democratic lawmakers.Democratic Representative Scott Peters, a longtime supporter of Afghan refugees, said the planned removals could put vulnerable people at serious risk."Afghans who stood with American troops, and their families, are being quietly loaded onto a plane to Pakistan, where they will very likely be pushed to the Taliban-controlled Afghanistan," Peters said in a statement.He accused the administration of potentially putting former allies and their families in danger."If this administration has its way, we would be throwing our vulnerable allies into the jaws of mortal danger. This is absolute cruelty and it is not who we are. This decision needs to be reversed," he added.The planned deportations have renewed concerns among Afghan refugee advocates about the future of people who sought safety in the United States after the Taliban returned to power following the withdrawal of American forces in 2021.You use AI every day. articles.title: Thousands rally in Berlin as Gen Z plans protests in 30 German cities
articles.summary: Demonstrations sweeping Europe are inspiring young Germans frustrated by rising costs of living amid military spending.
articles.body:
Berlin, Germany – Thousands of people are gathering in Berlin and more than 30 other German cities as the nation becomes the latest European country to be hit by a wave of student protests sweeping the continent.

Gathering at the Platz des 18 Maerz, on the west side of the capital’s iconic Brandenburg Gate on a sunny but chilly Saturday afternoon, there was support for the young people within a mixed demographic crowd.

Anti-fascist activists smoking hand-rolled cigarettes and wearing keffiyehs waited patiently alongside students dressed in Halloween outfits, smartly dressed grandmothers donning “omas gegen rechts” (grandmothers against the right) badges, and camera crews, ahead of the 2pm (13:00 GMT) rally start.

The protests were organised by a loose alliance called Gen Z Regelt (Gen Z sorts it), and by Saturday morning, nearly 180,000 people across 34 cities had signed up to participate – with the main host cities including Frankfurt, Cologne, Munich and the capital Berlin.

Nearly 12,000 people had signed up to join in the German capital, and people were continuing to stream into the square well into the demonstration to listen to speakers in what was so far a calm afternoon in the capital.

However, at a rally in the western city of Cologne, scuffles broke out between protesters and police, who moved in to contain a march there.

The protest organisers had outlined six key issues that took them to the streets on Saturday, including the rising cost of living, education cuts and military conscription.

Students told Al Jazeera that they are both angry and frustrated by ongoing funding cuts, even as the government invests heavily in the military.

Yet they also said they feel a sense of hope after seeing student protests in different parts of Europe in recent weeks.

Veronika Dinter travelled to Berlin on Friday night from Hannover to participate in the protest.

The 23-year-old political science student said that due to high living costs, she had to take on a part-time job to fund her studies.

“I wanted to start studying to develop critical thinking and learn something new, but I didn’t realise how much it would cost to do so. I think this is something a lot of people in my generation are experiencing right now,” she said.

“Funding for education and social services are being cut, while the cost of living keeps rising. Universities are struggling, institutes are closing, teachers are losing their jobs and education facilities are literally falling apart.

“This crisis is the political failure of our government. And instead of solving it, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his rich friends are funding the military with billions of euros.”

This is a sentiment that Emma Heymann, a 24-year-old student living in Berlin, resonated with.

“Our generation feels very angry at the government because they are making these huge cuts that are affecting our quality of life here. And at the same time, they are spending billions on the military and spending money to fund the genocide in Gaza,” she said.

Phil Tziartzianis travelled eight hours from his hometown of Kassel to join his friend Jan Chrominski and other young people at the demonstration.

“It feels important for me to be here among other young people who feel the same way,” he said.

The protesters join a wave of demonstrations that have swept across Europe in recent weeks, including in France, Belgium, Italy, Spain and Serbia.

Kilian Hampel is a senior research fellow at the Future of Work Lab at the University of Konstanz. He says other demonstrations are having an impact on young Germans.

“The frustration itself has been building for years, but this is definitely part of a wave we are seeing across Europe, and young people here are feeling that they can actually take their worries and problems to the streets,” he said. “Many of their concerns, in particular around poor educational infrastructure, are legitimate, and it’s important that they are listened to.”

The Berlin demonstration is expected to last two hours, with another one organised by a different alliance, planned at 5:30pm (16:30 GMT) in a different part of the German capital.

In the past week, political figures have raised concerns about the protests turning violent.

Yet demonstrators say they see the narrative of violence distracting from the issues they want to raise.

“We urge the police to not confront our demonstrations with any kind of violence,” Dinter, the student from Hannover, said.

“We stand in solidarity with all the people around the world who are fighting for an affordable life, for more investment in the education system, and against wars and military buildup.”

articles.title: ‘There is and was no other gun’: Mangione team argues double jeopardy bars state murder trial
articles.summary: Lawyers for Luigi Mangione on Friday continued to push for the dismissal of his state court murder and weapons case, arguing that his guilty plea to federal stalking charges two months ago bars a separate trial.
articles.body: Lawyers for Luigi Mangione on Friday continued to push for the dismissal of his state court murder and weapons case, arguing that his guilty plea to federal stalking charges two months ago bars a separate trial. Mangione, the admitted killer of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, pleaded guilty in Manhattan federal court in August. The plea set off a protracted battle over the future of the separate state court prosecution for second-degree murder and weapons possession. His state trial, slated to start Sept. 18, was postponed indefinitely so the court could take up whether double jeopardy applies. A decision on the dismissal motion is expected Dec. 10. Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s office maintains the state case can legally proceed because its charges differ substantially from those in the federal court case, which centered on stalking and crossing state lines and cyberstalking through use of interstate facilities, each resulting in death. The state indictment is a classic murder case, prosecutors argued, and murder is generally not defined by federal statutes. Mangione’s team countered Friday that the charges in the two cases are materially the same. They told New York Supreme Court Justice Gregory Carro that the federal offenses Mangione pleaded guilty to, interstate stalking resulting in death, involves overlapping legal elements. “Here, Mangione was charged by the federal grand jury with possession of the same firearm at the same time and at the same location as the People are charging here,” Mangione’s attorneys Karen Friedman Agnifilo, Marc Agnifilo and Jacob Kaplan argued in a letter to the court. “There is and was no other gun.” Mangione faces a potential life sentence when he returns to federal court on Dec. 18. If the state case goes forward, he faces a maximum of 25 years to life in prison. State prosecutors must overcome New York state double jeopardy law, which requires distinct “evils” between the two cases for the state matter to proceed, legal experts told NBC News. Mangione’s lawyers say the harms addressed in the state and federal cases are one and the same. “There is no basis to find such a difference, much less a sufficiently great difference as to fit within the narrow statutory exception,” they wrote in their most recent submission. Earlier this month, Bragg’s office pointed to a double jeopardy exception that could give it a path forward if Carro finds that there were unique “elements” charged in the state case. Lead prosecutor Joel Seidemann argued in a filing that earlier litigation in the federal proceeding shows the state charges are significantly different. U.S. District Judge Margaret Garnett determined that the stalking could not be considered violent under the law, a ruling that led to the dismissal of two counts that would have made Mangione eligible for the death penalty. The Justice Department had announced its intention to seek capital punishment before Garnett’s ruling. Mangione admitted to using a 3D-printed firearm to shoot Thompson outside of the midtown Hilton early on Dec. 4, 2024, as the executive walked from his nearby hotel to his company’s investor conference. The gunman ambushed Thompson, a Minnesota father of two, firing several times before fleeing and setting off an interstate manhunt. He was arrested five days later in Altoona, Pennsylvania, after patrons recognized him at a McDonald’s from photos circulated by the NYPD. The Ivy League-educated Maryland native, who comes from a prominent family, said in federal court that he was motivated by a personal grievance with the health insurance industry. Investigators have said he was never a UnitedHealthcare policyholder. His attorneys have argued that case’s notoriety led to overprosecution, with state and federal officials seeking credit by pursuing separate cases for the same event.

articles.title: 'It's been killing me!' Celebrity Traitors winners relieved the secret is out
articles.summary: The second series of the hit show reached its finale on Friday, attracting a whopping 11.2 million live viewers.
articles.body:
Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Celebrity Traitors final

The winners of Celebrity Traitors have said they are relieved that they no longer need to keep the biggest secret in British TV, as they reunited to celebrate their victory.

Actor Sebastian Croft and comedian Romesh Ranganathan were the last ones standing, with the two faithfuls splitting the £83,000 prize pot between their chosen charities.

"I am feeling good, it's so nice to finally be able to talk about it properly," Croft, known to pals as Bash, told BBC Newsbeat.

The second series of the hit BBC One show finished on Friday, after the original 21 celebs were whittled down to seven finalists.

Reuniting with Ranganathan on the comedian's BBC Radio 2 show on Saturday morning, Croft said they had been worried about being seen together in public before the final.

"We were having dinner and we're not exactly a likely duo and the whole restaurant was like, 'we like you on Traitors and hope you win'," he said.

Croft added that he had woken up on Saturday "with a light sense that I don't have to keep the secret anymore. It's been killing me".

Ranganathan, 48, started his show by saying: "Last night, I don't know if you're aware, was the finale of The Celebrity Traitors and I won."

He said he was "delighted to win" but admitted he probably wouldn't have done so without Croft convincing him to banish the last remaining traitor, King Kenny.

"It's taken the gloss off it slightly that everybody's saying, 'you better thank [Croft] every day for the rest of your life'," he added, with his typical deadpan-humour.

But 24-year-old Croft said he thought Ranganathan had played the game in a "lovely" way.

"People are seeing how smart you are and how you're actually so on it, and you're such a good judge of character," he praised.

The finale drew an average audience of 11.2 million live viewers, and that number will rise when fans catch up on iPlayer. Other recent episodes have been watched by more than 15 million, including catch-up.

"It's been a wild thing to be part of. To be on Uncloaked and sat with Romesh talking about winning was so surreal," Croft said, referencing the BBC's spin-off chat show.

"It's an out of body experience," he added.

Celebrity Traitors comes to a climax in nail-biting final

Croft said he "really wanted to be a traitor", but he turned out to be one of the strongest faithfuls after voting out Kenny - a tactical decision on how to play the show's famous endgame.

"The truth is, I didn't know for sure, but what you're trying to do isn't find a traitor, it's trying to get rid of everyone who isn't the most faithful," he explained.

"I think for both Maya [Jama] and Kenny there was no big thing where I was like 'they're obviously a traitor', but when you boil it down they haven't done anything that's really stuck out enough to make them obviously faithful."

Croft told Newsbeat that he gets why "people are obsessed with the show" and even his family had their own theories about how the game would go.

"So many people get so invested and it's lovely because it becomes so much bigger."

The final saw the celebs successfully banish the remaining traitors - Love Island host Maya Jama and YouTuber King Kenny.

But Kenny shocked viewers when he turned on his fellow traitor Jama at the final round table.

Asked if he's spoken to her since then, Kenny joked that "she's blocked me on everything", and then admitted that he had pre-warned her.

"I already told her that I was going to vote for her and she knew potentially that could be coming," he said.

"It was just too obvious, if I didn't go for her at that point, I think my time would've been coming even quicker than when I went out."

Kenny said he "experienced everything possible in the game" after starting out as a faithful, getting a shield to protect him from murder and then being recruited as a traitor.

But he said he "should have had a better plan for the final" and wasn't prepared for how hard it would be.

"There were so many times when I felt bad pinning stuff on people," he said. "It's a very draining thing to do as a traitor.

"There's moments when there is fun but lying to people for that long is insane, you build friendships as well and feel bad."

On his show, Ranganathan also asked fellow finalist, Little Mix singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock, about taking part in challenges while pregnant.

In the final episode, Pinnock was seen hanging off the side of a helicopter and lowering herself to the ground with a rope.

"I'm just super proud of myself," she said. "It's kind of just shown me that I really can do anything I put my mind to."

articles.title: Congo’s Ebola outbreak death toll crosses 5,000, half the total infected
articles.summary: The death toll from the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has crossed 5,000, with more than 10,000 people infected as the disease
articles.body: The death toll from the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has crossed 5,000, with more than 10,000 people infected as the disease continues to spread across the country and cases are reported in other African nations, the latest government data showed on Saturday.Data from the Congolese health ministry showed that 5,026 people had died among 10,351 reported infections, representing a fatality rate of nearly 50 per cent. The rising toll has raised concerns among health experts about the authorities' ability to contain the outbreak, AP reported.|The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, was declared in mid-May, taking authorities by surprise. Since then, health officials have struggled to contain its spread.It is now the second-deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, behind the two-year West African outbreak between 2014 and 2016, which killed 11,000 people across several countries.“It is a very tragic milestone because it is just not a number,” said Dr Patrick Otim, a programme area manager with the World Health Organisation (WHO), AP reported.“It is families and communities that have been devastated by this outbreak. The number also shows the severity of this outbreak.”A total of 2,788 people have reportedly recovered so far.The Bundibugyo virus has no known vaccine or treatment, and healthcare workers are treating patients based on their symptoms.Ebola spreads across Congo's provincesSince May, the outbreak has reached 67 of Congo's 178 health zones across eight of its 26 provinces. Fifty of the affected health zones continue to report active cases.The outbreak has been concentrated in the country's eastern region, particularly Ituri and North Kivu provinces, which together have recorded 9,782 confirmed cases and 4,792 deaths.Health authorities continue to face difficulties in contact tracing and testing, both considered essential to containing the spread of the virus.According to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, cited by the AP, around 80 per cent of new cases are emerging outside the chain of contacts being monitored by health officials.Around one-third of recorded deaths have also occurred outside treatment centres, before the victims could be tested for Ebola, WHO's Otim said.Conflict in eastern Congo complicates responseThe outbreak has placed additional pressure on efforts to contain the disease in a region already affected by conflict and insecurity.Eastern Congo, where the outbreak is concentrated, is the site of fighting between government forces and several armed groups, including the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group. An Islamist insurgency also operates in border areas with Uganda, where the Allied Democratic Forces carry out attacks.The security situation has restricted the reach of healthcare workers, complicating efforts to trace contacts, test suspected cases and provide timely treatment.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tear gas, water cannon, clashes: France hit by third weekend of protests
articles.summary: The French government on Saturday estimated that 320,000 people participated in nationwide protests against rising living costs and government policies,
articles.body: The French government on Saturday estimated that 320,000 people participated in nationwide protests against rising living costs and government policies, as demonstrations entered their third consecutive weekend.Fresh clashes broke out between police and protesters in Paris, where some demonstrators hurled paving stones and an incendiary device at security forces, prompting officers to fire tear gas, AFP reported.Tensions also flared in Marseille, Lyon and Toulouse, with police using tear gas and water cannon to disperse demonstrators. However, a coalition of youth organisations and student unions put the nationwide turnout at nearly 500,000, including 200,000 in Paris, significantly higher than the government's estimate of 70,000 in the French capital.The government had deployed around 70,000 police officers and gendarmes nationwide to manage the demonstrations and prevent further violence.Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had warned ahead of the protests that authorities faced a high risk of public disorder, particularly from groups seeking to turn demonstrations violent.The demonstrations also saw participants dressed as clowns and witches, reflecting the Halloween theme of Saturday's protests. Despite the largely peaceful nature of the marches, the fresh confrontations raised concerns over further violence during the nationwide mobilisation.The protests are driven by growing public anger over rising living costs, declining purchasing power, strained public services and dissatisfaction with government policies.What began as a student-led movement over poor school conditions, overcrowded classrooms and inadequate educational resources has expanded into a wider mobilisation involving trade unions, Yellow Vest activists and other groups.The demonstrations have also brought together people protesting against rising food, housing and fuel costs, as well as concerns over economic inequality and police violence.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Piprahwa Buddha relics arrive in Arunachal for Oct 31–Nov 20 exposition in Tawang, West Kameng, Namsai; Modi and Dalai Lama hail Buddhist heritage.
articles.body: Itanagar: Sacred Piprahwa relics linked with Buddha arrived in Arunachal Pradesh on Saturday for a three-week exposition beginning in Tawang, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi saying the event would provide devotees a rare opportunity to connect more deeply with Buddhist heritage and teachings.The sacred relics will be displayed across Tawang, West Kameng and Namsai districts from Oct 31 to Nov 20 with support from the Union ministry of culture.In messages marking the occasion, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the Dalai Lama highlighted Arunachal Pradesh’s important place in India’s Buddhist heritage and expressed hope that the exposition would strengthen people’s spiritual connection with Buddhism while promoting the values of peace, compassion and harmony.Modi said the Buddha’s teachings had guided humanity towards peace and compassion for more than two millennia and described Arunachal Pradesh as an integral part of India’s Buddhist heritage. He noted that Buddhist traditions had enriched the state’s spiritual and cultural life for centuries, with the Tawang Monastery remaining a prominent centre of Buddhist faith and learning.The Dalai Lama said he was pleased that devotees in Arunachal Pradesh had been given an opportunity to pay homage to the sacred relics of Buddha Shakyamuni.“The Buddha’s teachings can then be applied in daily life through a simple principle: if you can, help others; if you cannot, at least refrain from harming them,” the Dalai Lama said in his message.Recalling his visits to Arunachal Pradesh, the Dalai Lama said he had witnessed a steady growth in Buddhist studies and appreciation of the religion’s benefits among devotees in the state.Taking to X, Arunachal Pradesh CM Pema Khandu said he received the sacred relics at Tawang Air Force Station and expressed his gratitude to the IAF for safely transporting them from New Delhi. He also expressed gratitude to Modi and the Dalai Lama for their messages and good wishes.Khandu described the arrival of the sacred relics as a historic and spiritually significant occasion, saying the PM’s message recognised Arunachal Pradesh’s special place in India’s Buddhist heritage.Khandu invited devotees, scholars and visitors from across the country and abroad to participate in the exposition. articles.title: Chennai to have 36 new parks, 11 playgrounds by 2031
articles.summary: Chennai to add 36 new parks and 11 playgrounds by 2031 under CMIUDM, costing ₹44 crore, with tenders underway across multiple GCC zones.
articles.body: Chennai: The city will get 36 new parks and 11 playgrounds at around ₹44 crore, as Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) will develop them in the first phase of Chief Minister’s Integrated Urban Development Mission (CMIUDM).The projects come under the CMIUDM, a five-year mission launched by the state govt for 2026-2031, with an overall outlay of ₹1.5 lakh crore to improve infrastructure and civic amenities across urban local bodies. Of this, ₹2,000 crore has been earmarked over five years for urban greening, recreation and open spaces across the state’s urban local bodies.GCC commissioner G S Sameeran said the tender process for 36 parks at a cost of ₹34.45 crore and 11 playgrounds at ₹9.52 crore was underway. The new parks will come up across the city, in Manali, Tondiarpet, Alandur, Ambattur, Anna Nagar, Teynampet, Kodambakkam, Perungudi and Sholinganallur zones. The 11 playgrounds will be in Madhavaram, Tondiarpet, Kodambakkam and Sholinganallur.In Manali zone, new parks are planned at Sendhur Kumaran Nagar, Elandhanur, Periyar Nagar and Anbu Valarmathi Nagar. In Tondiarpet, a park is proposed beneath the 2B bridge on Manali Road, and parks will come up on CTH Road, Kumaran Nagar, Park Road, Gurusamy Street, Mogappair Industrial Estate and areas near Jeevan Bima Nagar in Ambattur.Other locations include the Kathipara–Airport gateway and VIP arrival/departure area in Alandur, Nelson Manickam Road, and Peters Road in Teynampet. In Perungudi, parks are planned along VGP 7th Cross Street, Sarathi Nagar 2nd Street and Balaji Nagar 19th Street. In Sholinganallur zone, several locations have been identified, including Kannagi Nagar’s 3rd and 4th Main Roads, Adithyaram Nagar and multiple TNUHDB streets.The need for additional green spaces is significant. Guidelines from the Union Ministry of Urban Development recommend 10-12 sq m of open space per person. However, the Chennai Metropolitan Area (CMA), which covers four corporations, has only about 2% of its geographical area classified as declared parks, according to the Second Master Plan for the Chennai Metropolitan Area, 2026 (Volume 3), published by Chennai Metropolitan Development Authority (CMDA). articles.title: Alternative routes, night-time movement prescribed for sugar cane transport in Kolhapur
articles.summary: Kolhapur police issue night-only (9pm–6am) sugarcane transport rules and diversion routes; reflectors mandatory, loudspeakers and overloading banned.
articles.body: Kolhapur: With the sugarcane crushing season underway, Kolhapur police have introduced alternative routes for sugarcane transport vehicles to prevent traffic congestion and accidents in the city.Superintendent of police Nilotpal has appealed to transporters operating trucks, tractor-trolleys and bullock carts to strictly follow the routes prescribed by the City Traffic Branch. He has also directed that sugarcane transportation within the city be restricted to night hours, between 9pm and 6am.Police will also take action against tractor-trolleys operating without reflectors and those fitted with loudspeakers playing music at high volumes.“Many tractors transporting sugarcane are fitted with loudspeakers. The loud music prevents drivers from hearing horns sounded by vehicles approaching from behind. The use of such speakers has been banned. Reflectors must also be installed at the rear of every vehicle and bullock cart to ensure visibility and prevent accidents. Overloaded vehicles will also face penal action,” Nilotpal said.As per the guidelines issued by the City Traffic Branch, vehicles heading towards Chhatrapati Rajaram Sugar Factory from Tawde Hotel will proceed via Tararani Statue, Sadar Bazar Chowk, Dhairya Prasad Hall Chowk, SP Office Chowk and Kasba Bawda. articles.title: Midnight bites: Of kebabs, coffee & conversations
articles.summary: Lucknow nightlife shifts later with midnight food trails, cafés, clubs and street bites at 1090, Food Valley, Gomti Nagar, Hazratganj and Old Lucknow.
articles.body: The kebabs are still sizzling, coffee machines are still humming, and the lights of food streets are far from dimming.At a time when the city once began winding down for the night, its youngsters are stepping out — for a plate of momos at 1090, coffee in Gomti Nagar, a late-night food run or music that carries them into midnight. The city has changed its bedtime and with it, its idea of nightlife.At Food Valley, tables remain occupied and groups of youngsters move from one counter to another. At 1090 Chatori Gali, friends gather around plates of momos, chaap and noodles. In Gomti Nagar, cafés have become places to sit long after dinner. And in the older parts of the city, kebabs and biryani continue to give the night its unmistakable Lucknow flavour.The city has not discovered nightlife overnight. It has simply changed what nightlife means.“Earlier, going out at night usually meant dinner with family or meeting friends for chai. Now youngsters have so many options that the night itself has become a part of their social life,” says a college student, Rohan Srivastava.For an older generation, a Lucknow evening meant kebabs in Chowk, a walk through Hazratganj, chai with friends or a late dinner before heading home. Today, the night can mean a food trail, coffee with friends, a live music performance, a club, a long drive or simply finding a corner where conversations can continue beyond midnight.FOOD VALLEY: WHERE DINNER BECOMES A PLANFood Valley has emerged as one of the city’s newer after-dark food destinations. What makes the place work at night is not just the food but the crowd — students, families, young professionals and groups of friends moving between stalls.“We usually come here after 9pm because everyone can find something they like. One wants momos, another wants dessert and someone else wants chai. It is easier than deciding on one restaurant,” says Aditi Verma, a college student.For many youngsters, that is the appeal of Food Valley. There is no need to book a table or plan an elaborate night out. You arrive, walk around and decide what the night tastes like.“Food Valley is more about hanging out than just eating. Even if we are not very hungry, we come here because there is always something happening,” says Kunal Mishra, a bank employee.1090 CHATORI GALI: THE OLD FAVOURITE THAT REFUSES TO FADEIf Food Valley represents the organised version of street-food nightlife, 1090 Chatori Gali retains the informality that made the area popular in the first place.The attraction after dark is simple — food, friends and movement.“I prefer 1090 at night because it doesn’t feel like a formal outing. We can meet, eat something, walk around and leave whenever we want,” said Shubham Tiwari, a young professional.For college students, the affordability is another attraction.“We don’t need a big budget for a night out here. We can order something, share it and spend time with friends. That is why we keep coming back,” says Niharika Singh, a university student.The stretch has also become a meeting point for people who may not necessarily be looking for a nightclub. For them, the crowd itself is part of the experience.SUMMIT BUILDING: WHERE LUCKNOW’S CLUB CULTURE FOUND A HOMEThen there is the other end of the spectrum.The Summit Building in Vibhuti Khand became the most visible symbol of Lucknow’s modern club culture, bringing several nightlife venues into one destination. For many young people, a night out now means DJs, dance floors, music and dressing up.“We come to Summit when we want to party. It is different from going to a cafe — you dress up, meet a bigger group and the night feels like an event,” says businessman Rishabh Khanna.For some, it is the atmosphere that matters.“At a cafe you sit and talk, but here the whole point is to dance and enjoy the music. It feels like a proper night out,” says designer Priya BansalHAZRATGANJ: WHERE THE NIGHT STILL HAS AN OLD-WORLD RHYTHMBefore cafes, food streets and clubs changed Lucknow’s after-dark map, there was Hazratganj. The city’s iconic boulevard was once the default evening plan — a stroll under the lights, window-shopping, chaat, ice cream or a stop for coffee before heading home. Even today, Ganj retains that leisurely charm, though the crowd and its reasons for being there have changed.“Hazratganj still feels different at night. You do not necessarily come here for one place; you come to walk, meet friends and soak in the atmosphere. It has a charm that newer nightlife spots cannot completely replace,” says Riya Mehrotra, a student.“We used to come to Hazratganj, walk around, have chai or ice cream and go home. There were fewer choices, but perhaps that was what made the evenings special,” a resident of Hazratganj, Anil Tandon, remarks.Shareeba Khan (53) says that for the younger generation, a Ganj evening is now often one stop in a longer night — coffee in the area, a drive towards Gomti Nagar or food at 1090. For older residents, however, the Ganj remains a reminder of a time when going out at night did not need an itinerary. The street may no longer be the whole of Lucknow’s nightlife, but it remains an important part of its story — the old evening that stayed on even as the city learnt to stay out later.OLD LUCKNOWYet for all the cafes, clubs and food streets, the city’s oldest nightlife tradition remains remarkably intact.In Chowk and other parts of Old Lucknow, the night still belongs to kebabs, biryani, chai and conversations.“Our nightlife has always been food. Earlier we would go out for kebabs and come back. Now youngsters have more options, but food is still the common point,” says Farooq Ahmad, a retired engineer.For younger residents too, the old city remains part of the night map.“You can go to a cafe or a club, but if you want to experience Lucknow, you still end up talking about kebabs, biryani and the old city. That has not changed,” says Yash Agarwal, a student.Raghav Arora (62) says that is what makes Lucknow’s nightlife different. The city has not replaced its old night with a new one. It has layered the new over the old. A youngster can spend the evening at a cafe, move to 1090 for street food, head to a club and still finish the night searching for a kebab.GOMTI NAGAR: THE CITY’S NEW NIGHT-TIME CENTREGomti Nagar has emerged as one of the most visible centres of Lucknow’s changing nightlife. What was once largely a commercial and residential extension of the city now stays active well after dinner, with restaurants, lounges, food outlets and entertainment spaces drawing young professionals and students.The difference is not simply that places remain open later. It is that people now step out specifically because the night offers something to do. Places such as Tickle Pink, Bar Stock Exchange and Boho Bar, Red Dragon and DLF MyPad have added to the area’s after-dark options, giving youngsters spaces ranging from casual outings and food to music, drinks and late-night socialising.“For us, going out at night is not necessarily about partying. Sometimes we just want to drive around, eat something and spend time outside. Gomti Nagar gives us enough options to do that,” says Arjun Malhotra, an employee at a private firm.The area’s nightlife is also closely tied to the city’s expanding work culture, with young employees often meeting after office hours rather than during the day. For many, the plan is no longer simply dinner and home — the night can stretch across several stops, from a meal to a bar or lounge and a late-night drive.AFTER DARK, A SECOND CASH WINDOWFor many small food sellers and shopkeepers in Lucknow, the night is no longer just an extension of business hours — it has become a separate earning window. Vendors operating around food streets, cafes and busy evening stretches say the late-night crowd can bring in a significant share of their daily income, with some making several thousand rupees during the night depending on the location and day.“Once it gets dark, customers keep coming. On a busy night, we can make around Rs 3,000 to Rs 5,000 from the evening and late-night crowd,” said Imran Khan, a food vendor.“People come out after dinner for chai, snacks, desserts and quick bites. We keep the shop open because there is money to be made even late at night. articles.title: Over 10,000 run to spread message of unity, Nagpur athlete wins 21km race
articles.summary: Over 10,000 join NMC’s Unity Marathon in Nagpur for Patel Jayanti; Ethiopian Tsehay Aohava wins women’s 21km, Rajan Yadav tops men’s.
articles.body: Nagpur: From an 84-year-old defying age to an Ethiopian athlete racing to victory, Nagpur’s streets witnessed a celebration of endurance, sporting spirit and national unity on Saturday as over 10,000 runners participated in the Unity Marathon organised by Nagpur Municipal Corporation (NMC) to mark Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel’s birth anniversary.While Ethiopian athlete Tsehay Aohava clinched the women’s 21km title, Nagpur’s Rajan Yadav emerged victorious in the men’s category, giving the home crowd a reason to cheer. The marathon, which began at Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Ground in Lakadganj, attracted participants from Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Delhi, besides international competitors.Yadav completed the 21km race in 1:01:58 to finish ahead of Uttar Pradesh’s Satish Kumar Verma (1:02:24) and Rajasthan’s Mukesh Bhanu (1:03:05). In the women’s category, Aohava clocked 1:15:02, followed by Nagpur’s Yamini Thakre (1:16:18) and Ratnagiri’s Sakshi (1:17:42).One of the day’s biggest attractions was 84-year-old Shripad Burde, who completed the run, earning applause from dignitaries and fellow participants. Young children also added colour to the event through a fancy dress competition, portraying historical and religious personalities.Nagpur athletes dominated several short-distance categories. Gaurav Khodtkar won the men’s 10km race in 29 minutes and 20 seconds, narrowly beating Dheeraj Kumar, who finished just two seconds behind. Mitali Bhoyar topped the women’s 5.3km category, while Umred’s Sumit Meshram won the boys’ under-16 5.3km race.
